hook: Aravind Srinivas earned an undergraduate degree from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras before moving to the United States for a PhD in computer science at UC Berkeley, completed in 2021, where his research focused on reinforcement learning and self-supervised representation learning. After graduating he worked briefly as a research scientist at OpenAI and then at Google DeepMind. In August 2022 he co-founded Perplexity AI with Denis Yarats, Johnny Ho, and Andy Konwinski, building what the company calls an answer engine that searches the web in real time and returns cited, sourced responses rather than a list of links. As CEO, he has positioned Perplexity as a search-grounded alternative to traditional chatbots and search engines since the product's public launch in December 2022.

reading.body:
Aravind Srinivas moved from research scientist roles at OpenAI and Google DeepMind directly to founding Perplexity AI in August 2022, positioning a search-grounded answer engine as an alternative to both traditional search and chatbots.

The timeline shows a common path for AI founders: PhD in a specialized subfield, a short apprenticeship at a leading lab, then immediate company launch. Srinivas trained in reinforcement learning and self-supervised representation learning at Berkeley before spending months at two of the field's top research institutions. This pattern suggests that foundational AI capability, rather than years of operational experience, is treated as sufficient preparation for starting a company in this space.

Perplexity's product category matters more than most startups in this ecosystem. The company does not attempt to replace general-purpose LLMs or build new model architectures. It applies existing language models to a specific problem: real-time search with citations. This is computationally lighter than training new foundation models, which explains why the founders could move from research to launch in less than a year. The product depends on compute already deployed elsewhere, not on building new scale.

The data does not cover Perplexity's infrastructure costs, power consumption, or capital raised. It does not explain how the company acquires or allocates compute, or whether search-grounded systems face different power constraints than chatbots. Those gaps matter for understanding whether this business model avoids or simply defers the building and power constraints that bind larger AI operations.
